title: Scalp, Face, Parotid & Jaw
summary: The soft tissues of the scalp and face, the muscles that move them, and the jaw joint.

lessons.title: Layers of the Scalp and the Danger Zone

levels.kid:
Your scalp is the skin and padding on top of your head. It is made of five layers, stacked like a sandwich. A trick to remember them is the word **SCALP**: Skin, Connective tissue, Aponeurosis (a tough flat sheet), Loose tissue, and Pericranium (a thin cover glued to the skull bone).

The top three layers stick together like one thick blanket. Under them is a slippery, loose layer. That is why the scalp can slide around when you wiggle your forehead.

Doctors call that loose layer the **danger zone**. Germs that get in there can spread across the head, and there are tiny veins that lead inside to the brain. So doctors clean scalp cuts very carefully.
levels.hs:
The **scalp** is the soft tissue covering the top of the skull, from the eyebrows to the back of the head. Its five layers spell **SCALP**:

- **S**kin: thick and hairy, with many sweat and oil glands.
- **C**onnective tissue: dense and fatty, packed with the scalp's arteries, veins and nerves.
- **A**poneurosis: the **galea aponeurotica**, a tough sheet that links the frontalis muscle in front to the occipitalis muscle at the back.
- **L**oose areolar tissue: a thin, spongy layer that lets the top three layers glide.
- **P**ericranium: the outer covering (periosteum) of the skull bones.

The first three layers move as one unit. Surgeons call this unit the scalp proper and peel it off along the loose layer.

Two features matter clinically. First, the scalp **bleeds heavily**. In the dense connective layer, the vessel walls are held open, so cut arteries cannot easily clamp shut. Even small cuts can bleed a lot.

Second, layer 4 is called the **danger zone**. Infection or blood can spread easily through it. It also contains **emissary veins**, which have no valves and connect scalp veins to the venous sinuses inside the skull. Bacteria can travel through them to cause meningitis or a sinus clot. Example: a dirty scalp wound that reaches the loose layer needs careful cleaning and closure.
levels.college:
The scalp extends from the supraorbital margins to the external occipital protuberance and superior nuchal lines, and laterally to the zygomatic arches. Its five layers (**SCALP**) have distinct clinical behavior.

- **Skin**: the thickest skin on the head, with abundant hair follicles and sebaceous glands. It is a common site for sebaceous (pilar) cysts.
- **Connective tissue (dense)**: fibrous septa tie the skin to the galea and enclose fat lobules, nerves and vessels. Because vessel adventitia is anchored to these septa, severed vessels gape and bleed profusely. Galeal tension also pulls wound edges apart.
- **Aponeurosis (galea aponeurotica)**: the epicranial aponeurosis linking the frontal and occipital bellies of occipitofrontalis; laterally it thins over the temporal fascia. A scalp laceration that gapes wide means the galea is cut, and it is usually repaired to control bleeding and restore strength.
- **Loose areolar tissue**: the **subaponeurotic (subgaleal) space**, the "danger area." It is bounded anteriorly by the frontalis attachment to the eyebrow skin (it does not reach bone), posteriorly by the superior nuchal lines, and laterally by the zygomatic arches. Fluid can therefore track forward into the eyelids, producing periorbital bruising ("black eyes") after scalp trauma.
- **Pericranium**: firmly adherent at sutures, so a subperiosteal collection is limited to a single bone.

**Blood supply** comes from both carotid systems. The internal carotid supplies the scalp through the supratrochlear and supraorbital arteries. The external carotid supplies it through the superficial temporal, posterior auricular and occipital arteries. These vessels anastomose richly and enter from the periphery, so pedicled scalp flaps are based inferiorly.

**Emissary veins** (parietal, mastoid, occipital) run through the danger zone, crossing the skull to reach the dural venous sinuses. They have no functional valves, so infection in the subgaleal space can spread intracranially, causing osteomyelitis, meningitis, epidural abscess or septic dural sinus thrombosis.

**Lymph** drains to the occipital, mastoid (retroauricular), parotid and submandibular nodes.
levels.phd:
The scalp's layered architecture gives each layer different mechanical and infectious behavior, and many neurosurgical decisions follow from it.

**Hemostatic biology.** In the dense subcutaneous layer, vessel adventitia is fused to fibrous septa. Reflex vasoconstriction still occurs, but the lumen cannot collapse, so bleeding is profuse. Rich anastomoses across the midline and between internal and external carotid territories mean that tying a single feeding vessel rarely stops bleeding. This is why galea-inclusive closure, Raney clips during craniotomy and local infiltration with vasoconstrictors are used.

**Galeal mechanics.** The galea carries most of the scalp's tensile strength and resists stretching. This limits primary closure of large defects. Galeotomies (relaxing incisions parallel to tension lines) gain small increments of advancement. Tissue expanders exploit the galea's slow stretch (creep) for reconstruction, as seen in burn alopecia.

**Neonatal compartment anatomy.** Birth-related collections separate cleanly by layer:
- **Caput succedaneum**: edema in the subcutaneous layer that crosses sutures and resolves in days.
- **Cephalohematoma**: subperiosteal blood confined by sutural attachment of the pericranium, so it does not cross sutures.
- **Subgaleal hemorrhage**: bleeding into the danger zone after emissary vein rupture, often linked to vacuum extraction. Because the space runs from the orbits to the nape, a neonate can lose a large share of blood volume, causing hypovolemic shock and consumptive coagulopathy. Mortality figures historically quoted reach roughly 12-25%.

**Infection routes.** Emissary veins, like diploic and dural sinus systems, form a largely valveless network in which flow depends on pressure gradients. Subgaleal abscess can therefore produce septic thrombophlebitis, epidural empyema or superior sagittal sinus thrombosis. **Pott's puffy tumor**, a frontal subperiosteal abscess with osteomyelitis secondary to frontal sinusitis, illustrates a related bone-to-scalp route. It often coexists with intracranial empyema, especially in adolescents.

**Innervation.** The scalp is supplied by branches of CN V1 (supratrochlear, supraorbital), V2 (zygomaticotemporal) and V3 (auriculotemporal), and by C2-C3 (greater and lesser occipital, third occipital, great auricular). These nerves run in the dense layer, superficial to the galea, which is the basis for regional scalp blocks.
levels.expert:
Clinically, the scalp is a planning problem. Incisions, flaps and closures must respect its vascular supply, its nerves and the subgaleal plane.

**Incision and flap design.** Flaps should keep a broad, inferior base containing a named artery. For a frontotemporal (pterional) flap, that artery is the superficial temporal artery. Placing the incision about 1 cm anterior to the tragus and behind the hairline protects the STA trunk and the frontal branch of the facial nerve. Interfascial or subfascial dissection protects the frontal branch (detailed in the facial nerve lesson). Reopening prior incisions, irradiated scalp, and a bevacizumab history all raise wound-breakdown risk. Incisions that cross an old flap's base can devascularize skin islands.

**Pericranial flap.** Because the subgaleal plane separates the galea from the pericranium, a vascularized pericranial flap can be raised on the supraorbital and supratrochlear vessels. It is a workhorse for repairing anterior skull base defects and covering the frontal sinus after bifrontal craniotomy, reducing CSF leak and infection. Preserving it during the opening is a decision made before the first cut.

**Trauma pitfalls.**
- Scalp lacerations can cause substantial blood loss in children and anticoagulated adults. Prompt galea-inclusive closure or staples, rather than prolonged packing, is the priority.
- Palpating a laceration's edge can mimic a depressed fracture, and a firm subgaleal hematoma rim can do the same. CT resolves this.
- In neonates, a fluctuant collection crossing sutures with a falling hematocrit is subgaleal hemorrhage until proven otherwise. It demands serial head-circumference measurement and coagulation monitoring.

**Regional anesthesia.** Scalp blocks targeting six nerves on each side (supraorbital, supratrochlear, zygomaticotemporal, auriculotemporal, greater and lesser occipital) allow awake craniotomy for language and motor mapping. They also blunt the hemodynamic response to pin fixation.

**Reconstruction frontiers.** Small defects close with rotation flaps. Large defects need tissue expansion or free flaps (latissimus dorsi, anterolateral thigh) anastomosed to the STA or neck vessels. Exposed cranioplasty hardware, especially titanium mesh under thin irradiated scalp, remains a frequent failure mode. Open questions include optimal timing of radiotherapy relative to cranioplasty and the role of acellular dermal matrices in reinforcing thin scalp.

keyPoints: The scalp has five layers: Skin, Connective tissue, Aponeurosis, Loose areolar tissue, Pericranium
The top three layers move as one unit over the loose layer
Vessels held open in the dense connective layer make scalp cuts bleed heavily
The loose areolar (subgaleal) layer is the danger zone because blood and infection spread there
Valveless emissary veins let scalp infection reach the dural venous sinuses
Subgaleal hemorrhage crosses sutures; cephalohematoma is limited by them

test.q: In the SCALP mnemonic, what does the letter A stand for?
test.explain: A is the aponeurosis, the galea aponeurotica. The arachnoid is a meninx inside the skull, not a scalp layer.

test.q: Which scalp layer is called the danger zone?
test.explain: The loose areolar (subgaleal) layer lets blood and infection spread widely, and it contains emissary veins.

test.q: Why do scalp lacerations bleed so heavily?
choices: Vessel walls are held open by fibrous septa
Scalp blood has fewer clotting factors
The scalp contains no small arteries
test.explain: In the dense connective layer, vessel adventitia is anchored to septa, so cut vessels cannot collapse and gape open.

test.q: Emissary veins are dangerous in scalp infections because they:
choices: Drain the scalp into the parotid gland
Carry arterial blood to the face
Connect to sinuses and lack valves
test.explain: Valveless emissary veins link scalp veins to the dural venous sinuses, so infection can spread inside the skull.

test.q: The galea aponeurotica connects which two muscle bellies?
test.explain: The epicranial aponeurosis joins the frontal and occipital bellies of occipitofrontalis.

test.q: Blood in the subgaleal space can produce black eyes because:
choices: The space connects directly with the orbit bones
The pericranium is absent over the forehead
Frontalis inserts into skin, not bone, in front
Emissary veins drain into the eyelids
test.explain: Since frontalis attaches to eyebrow skin rather than bone, there is no bony barrier, so fluid tracks forward into the eyelids.

test.q: Which birth-related collection is limited by the skull sutures?
test.explain: A cephalohematoma is subperiosteal, and the pericranium attaches firmly at sutures, so the blood stays over one bone.

test.q: Which artery supplying the scalp comes from the internal carotid system?
test.explain: The supraorbital and supratrochlear arteries arise via the ophthalmic artery from the internal carotid. The others are external carotid branches.

test.q: Why are pedicled scalp flaps usually based inferiorly?
choices: Scalp arteries enter from the periphery
Veins drain upward toward the vertex
The galea is thickest at the vertex
Hair grows better on lower flaps
test.explain: The main scalp arteries rise from the periphery toward the vertex, so a lower base keeps the blood supply.

test.q: The outermost covering of the skull bones, the fifth scalp layer, is the ___.
test.explain: The pericranium is the periosteum on the outer surface of the skull.

test.q: What is the Latin-derived name for the tough fibrous sheet that forms the third scalp layer?
test.explain: The galea aponeurotica, or epicranial aponeurosis, gives the scalp most of its strength.

test.q: Veins crossing the skull from the scalp to the dural sinuses are called ___ veins.
test.explain: Emissary veins pass through skull foramina and lack functional valves.

kidTest.q: How many layers does the scalp have?
kidTest.explain: The scalp has five layers, one for each letter of SCALP.

kidTest.q: Which layer lets the scalp slide around?
kidTest.explain: The loose, slippery layer lets the top three layers glide.

kidTest.q: Why do doctors call the loose layer the danger zone?
choices: It is very hard to see
kidTest.explain: Germs can spread there and travel through tiny veins toward the brain.

kidTest.q: What is the pericranium?
choices: A thin cover on the bone
kidTest.explain: The pericranium is a thin cover glued to the skull bone.

kidTest.q: The five-letter memory word for the layers on top of your head is S _ _ _ _.
kidTest.explain: SCALP: Skin, Connective tissue, Aponeurosis, Loose tissue, Pericranium.

advancedTest.q: A neonate after vacuum delivery has a fluctuant swelling crossing sutures and a falling hematocrit. The best explanation is:
choices: Subgaleal hemorrhage in a space spanning orbits to nape
Epidural hematoma compressing the underlying dura
Caput succedaneum from edema in the dense layer
advancedTest.explain: The subgaleal space is large and unbounded by sutures, so emissary vein bleeding can cause hypovolemia. Caput crosses sutures but is edema and does not lower the hematocrit.

advancedTest.q: Ligating one feeding artery rarely stops a scalp hemorrhage because:
choices: Emissary veins supply most scalp blood
Scalp arteries lie beneath the pericranium
The galea itself contains the main arteries
Rich anastomoses join both carotid territories
advancedTest.explain: Extensive anastomoses across the midline and between internal and external carotid branches keep supplying the wound.

advancedTest.q: Why must a surgeon decide on a pericranial flap before opening for bifrontal craniotomy?
choices: Incising into the subgaleal plane can preserve it
It becomes adherent to the galea after exposure
Its blood supply comes from emissary veins
It is raised on the superficial temporal artery
advancedTest.explain: The subgaleal plane separates galea from pericranium, so dissecting there keeps a vascularized pericranial flap on supraorbital and supratrochlear vessels for skull base repair.

advancedTest.q: Scalp blocks can be placed superficially for awake craniotomy mainly because the scalp nerves:
choices: Arise wholly from the facial nerve
Travel beneath the pericranium on bone
Pass through the loose areolar danger zone
Run within the dense layer above the galea
advancedTest.explain: The sensory nerves (V1, V2, V3 branches and C2-C3) course in the dense connective layer, superficial to the galea, so they are reachable with superficial injections.

lessons.title: Muscles of Facial Expression

levels.kid:
Smile at a mirror. Now frown. Now puff your cheeks. Every one of those faces is made by tiny muscles just under your skin.

Most muscles pull on bones to move your arms and legs. Face muscles are special. Many of them pull on your **skin**. That is why your face can show happy, sad, surprised or grumpy so quickly.

There is a ring-shaped muscle around each eye that helps you blink and squeeze your eyes shut. Another ring goes around your lips so you can whistle and kiss. A flat cheek muscle helps you blow out birthday candles.

All these muscles get their messages from one nerve on each side, called the **facial nerve**. It is like a phone line telling your face what to do.
levels.hs:
The **muscles of facial expression** (also called **mimetic muscles**) are thin muscles in the superficial fascia of the face and scalp. Unlike most skeletal muscles, many attach to **skin** rather than only to bone, so when they contract they move the skin and create expressions.

They are grouped around the openings of the face:
- **Around the eye**: **orbicularis oculi** closes the eyelids, gently for blinking or tightly for squinting. **Corrugator supercilii** pulls the eyebrows together into a frown.
- **Around the mouth**: **orbicularis oris** closes and purses the lips. **Zygomaticus major** pulls the mouth corner up and out in a smile. **Depressor anguli oris** pulls it down.
- **Cheek**: **buccinator** presses the cheek against the teeth, keeping food between the teeth and helping you blow.
- **Scalp and forehead**: the **frontalis** (part of occipitofrontalis) raises the eyebrows and wrinkles the forehead.
- **Neck**: the **platysma**, a broad sheet, tenses the skin of the neck.

All of them are supplied by the **facial nerve (cranial nerve VII)**. They come from the **second pharyngeal arch** in the embryo, which explains why one nerve controls them all.

Real example: in **Bell's palsy**, the facial nerve on one side stops working. The person cannot close that eye, the forehead stays smooth, and the smile droops on that side.
levels.college:
The facial muscles develop from mesoderm of the **second (hyoid) pharyngeal arch** and migrate over the face, scalp and neck, dragging their nerve, the **facial nerve (CN VII)**, with them. They lie in the **superficial fascia**, have no deep fascial covering, and typically run from bone or fascia to the dermis. Their primary job is controlling the **orifices** (eyes, mouth, nose), with expression as a byproduct.

**Orbital group**
- **Orbicularis oculi**: *palpebral part* (in the lids, gentle blinking) and *orbital part* (forceful closure). A small *lacrimal part* aids tear drainage toward the lacrimal sac.
- **Corrugator supercilii**: vertical glabellar frown lines.
- **Procerus**: horizontal lines over the nasal bridge.

**Nasal group**: **nasalis** (compresses and flares the nostrils) and **depressor septi nasi**.

**Oral group**
- **Orbicularis oris**: sphincter of the lips.
- Elevators: **levator labii superioris**, **levator labii superioris alaeque nasi**, **zygomaticus major and minor**, **levator anguli oris**.
- Depressors: **depressor anguli oris**, **depressor labii inferioris**, **mentalis** (elevates and protrudes the lower lip, wrinkles the chin).
- **Risorius**: lateral pull.
- **Buccinator**: arises from the maxilla, mandible and **pterygomandibular raphe**. It is pierced by the **parotid duct** opposite the upper second molar.

Many oral muscles converge just lateral to the mouth corner at the **modiolus**, a fibromuscular knot.

**Other**: **occipitofrontalis** (frontal and occipital bellies joined by the **galea aponeurotica**), **auricular muscles**, and **platysma**.

**Innervation pattern**: motor fibres from CN VII emerge at the stylomastoid foramen and reach most muscles on their **deep surfaces**. The exceptions are three deep-lying muscles, **buccinator, levator anguli oris and mentalis**, which are innervated on their superficial surfaces. **Sensation** from the facial skin travels in the **trigeminal nerve (CN V)**, not CN VII.
levels.phd:
Phylogenetically, the mimetic muscles derive from the **sphincter colli** and platysma-like sheets of early mammals. Their expansion from a hyoid-arch muscle plate into discrete facial muscles parallels the evolution of suckling (buccinator, orbicularis oris) and social signalling in primates. In the embryo, second-arch myogenic precursors express **Tbx1** and **Pitx2** rather than the Pax3-dependent somitic program. Their connective tissue and patterning come from **cranial neural crest**, which governs where the muscles attach. Second-arch defects are therefore reflected in facial weakness, as in **Möbius syndrome** (CN VI and VII hypoplasia) and **hemifacial microsomia**.

Structurally, mimetic muscles are unusual skeletal muscles. They lack muscle spindles or have very few, and they rely heavily on cutaneous afferents via CN V for feedback. Their fibres are small and interdigitate with the dermis and the **superficial musculoaponeurotic system (SMAS)**, which is continuous with the temporoparietal fascia, galea and platysma. The SMAS transmits muscle force over broad areas of skin.

**Central control** is dual. The **facial motor nucleus** in the caudal pons has subnuclei arranged somatotopically. The neurons serving the upper face (frontalis, upper orbicularis oculi) receive substantial **bilateral corticobulbar** input, whereas the lower-face neurons receive mainly **contralateral** input. This explains the clinical distinction between an upper motor neuron lesion, which **spares the forehead**, and a lower motor neuron lesion (nucleus or nerve), which paralyses the whole hemiface. Recent tracing in primates (Morecraft and colleagues) shows that this bilaterality arises partly from cingulate and supplementary motor projections and is not simply symmetric.

Voluntary and emotional expression also dissociate. Patients with capsular strokes may be unable to smile on command but smile symmetrically at a joke, reflecting **extrapyramidal/limbic** pathways. The opposite pattern, **emotional facial paresis**, follows thalamic or insular lesions.

**Duchenne de Boulogne** (1862) used electrical stimulation to show that a genuine smile recruits **orbicularis oculi** along with zygomaticus major (the "Duchenne smile"). Ekman and Friesen later built on this work in the **Facial Action Coding System (FACS)**, which codes expressions as action units, for example AU6 (cheek raiser, orbicularis oculi) and AU12 (lip corner puller, zygomaticus major).
levels.expert:
Clinically, facial muscle anatomy is assessed by function, and the key bedside task is **localization**. Corneal exposure is the most urgent risk in facial palsy. Loss of orbicularis oculi produces **lagophthalmos** and a failed blink, and **Bell's phenomenon** (upward eye rolling on attempted closure) determines how protected the cornea is. Lower lid ectropion and epiphora follow because the lid loses tone and the lacrimal pump fails. Management includes lubrication and taping, and in persistent cases **gold or platinum upper-lid weights**, tarsorrhaphy or canthoplasty.

Grading uses the **House-Brackmann scale (I-VI)**, still the standard after vestibular schwannoma surgery. The **Sunnybrook** and the eFACE systems capture regional and synkinetic detail better. Prognosis after nerve injury is refined by **electroneuronography** within about 3-14 days; more than 90% degeneration predicts a poor spontaneous recovery.

**Aberrant regeneration** after Bell's palsy or surgical injury causes **synkinesis**: the eye closes during smiling, or the platysma tightens during speech. A related misrouting of parasympathetic fibres produces "crocodile tears" (gustatory lacrimation). Synkinesis is treated with targeted **botulinum toxin A** chemodenervation and neuromuscular retraining. The toxin blocks acetylcholine release by cleaving SNAP-25, and the same mechanism underlies its use in **hemifacial spasm** (often from vascular compression at the CN VII root exit zone, treated definitively by microvascular decompression) and **blepharospasm**. Spread of toxin into levator palpebrae, which is supplied by CN III, causes ptosis, a classic pitfall of periorbital injection.

For reanimation of a chronically paralysed face, the important fact is that denervated mimetic muscle becomes non-reinnervatable after roughly 12-24 months of motor endplate loss. Before that window closes, nerve transfers can be used: **masseteric-to-facial** (fast, strong, but requires learning to smile by biting), **hypoglossal-facial**, or **cross-face nerve grafts** (spontaneous, emotional smile but weaker). After it closes, the surgeon must bring in new muscle, such as a **free gracilis transfer** or **lengthening temporalis myoplasty**. These are aimed above all at restoring the **zygomaticus major** vector and the modiolus.

Open questions include objective, automated grading using FACS-based computer vision, and whether early corticosteroids plus antivirals add meaningful benefit over steroids alone in severe Bell's palsy.

keyPoints: Facial expression muscles lie in superficial fascia and many insert into skin
They develop from the second pharyngeal arch, so CN VII supplies them all
Orbicularis oculi closes the eye; orbicularis oris closes the lips
Buccinator keeps food between the teeth and is pierced by the parotid duct
Skin sensation of the face comes from CN V, not CN VII
Upper motor neuron lesions spare the forehead; lower motor neuron lesions do not

test.q: Which nerve supplies motor innervation to the muscles of facial expression?
test.explain: CN VII, the nerve of the second pharyngeal arch, supplies all mimetic muscles. The trigeminal nerve carries facial sensation and supplies the chewing muscles.

test.q: From which embryonic structure do the facial expression muscles develop?
test.explain: They come from the second (hyoid) arch, which is why the arch nerve, CN VII, innervates them.

test.q: Which muscle closes the eyelids?
test.explain: Orbicularis oculi is the eyelid sphincter. Corrugator draws the brows together, and frontalis raises them.

test.q: Which muscle presses the cheek against the teeth to keep food between them?
test.explain: Buccinator compresses the cheek. Masseter is a chewing muscle supplied by CN V, not a muscle of expression.

test.q: Which structure pierces the buccinator?
test.explain: The parotid duct pierces buccinator to open opposite the upper second molar.

test.q: Which muscle pulls the mouth corner up and out during a smile?
test.explain: Zygomaticus major is the main smile muscle. Depressor anguli oris pulls the mouth corner down.

test.q: A patient cannot wrinkle the forehead on one side and cannot close that eye. The lesion most likely affects:
test.explain: Paralysis of the whole hemiface, forehead included, indicates a lower motor neuron lesion of CN VII, as in Bell's palsy. A cortical lesion spares the forehead.

test.q: Where do many oral muscles converge just lateral to the corner of the mouth?
test.explain: The modiolus is the fibromuscular knot where several lip muscles meet. The raphe is an attachment for buccinator.

test.q: Light touch on the skin of the cheek is carried by which nerve?
test.explain: Facial skin sensation travels in CN V. CN VII is motor to the facial muscles.

test.q: The broad sheet of facial expression muscle that tenses the skin of the neck is the ___.
test.explain: The platysma lies in the superficial fascia of the neck and is supplied by the cervical branch of CN VII.

test.q: Name the sphincter muscle that closes and purses the lips.
test.explain: Orbicularis oris encircles the mouth and closes the lips.

test.q: The frontal and occipital bellies of occipitofrontalis are joined by the galea ___.
test.explain: The galea aponeurotica is the tough sheet linking the two bellies across the scalp.

kidTest.q: Many face muscles pull on your:
kidTest.explain: Face muscles pull on skin, which is why your face can show feelings.

kidTest.q: What does the ring muscle around your eye help you do?
kidTest.explain: The ring around the eye closes the eyelids so you can blink.

kidTest.q: Which muscle helps you blow out birthday candles?
kidTest.explain: The flat cheek muscle pushes air out when you blow.

kidTest.q: What tells your face muscles what to do?
kidTest.explain: The facial nerve is like a phone line that sends messages to your face muscles.

kidTest.q: A ring muscle goes around your lips so you can whistle and k _ _ _.
kidTest.explain: The lip ring muscle closes and puckers your lips.

advancedTest.q: A stroke patient has a drooping lower face on one side but can raise both eyebrows normally. The best explanation is:
choices: The frontalis is supplied by the trigeminal nerve rather than the facial
The lesion lies in the facial nerve distal to the stylomastoid foramen
The upper facial nucleus neurons receive bilateral corticobulbar input
The forehead muscles lack motor endplates and resist denervation
advancedTest.explain: Upper-face neurons get input from both hemispheres, so a unilateral cortical lesion spares the forehead. A distal nerve lesion would paralyse the forehead too.

advancedTest.q: A capsular stroke patient cannot smile on command but smiles symmetrically at a joke. This shows:
choices: Compensation by the trigeminal motor nucleus
Recovery of the facial nerve by aberrant regeneration
Separate pathways for voluntary and emotional expression
A lower motor neuron lesion that spares the nucleus
advancedTest.explain: Emotional smiles use limbic and extrapyramidal routes that bypass the damaged voluntary corticobulbar pathway.

advancedTest.q: Patients with facial palsy of more than about two years usually need free muscle transfer rather than nerve transfer because:
choices: Masseteric nerve fibres degenerate after the first year
Cross-face grafts provide too much strength over time
Denervated mimetic muscle loses its motor endplates
The stylomastoid foramen closes by bony remodelling
advancedTest.explain: After roughly 12-24 months, denervated facial muscle can no longer be reinnervated, so new muscle such as gracilis must be brought in.

advancedTest.q: After botulinum toxin injection for blepharospasm, a patient develops ptosis. The most likely mechanism is:
choices: Blockade of trigeminal sensory input from the eyelid
Stimulation of synkinetic regrowth in the facial nerve
Toxin spread to orbicularis oculi causing extra weakness
Toxin spread to levator palpebrae, supplied by CN III
advancedTest.explain: Ptosis means failure of lid elevation, which depends on levator palpebrae (CN III). Orbicularis weakness would impair lid closure, not elevation.

lessons.title: The Parotid Gland and Extracranial Branches of the Facial Nerve

levels.kid:
In front of each ear, just under your cheek skin, is a soft gland called the **parotid gland**. It is the biggest of your spit glands. When you smell pizza and your mouth waters, the parotid helps make that spit.

The spit travels through a little tube that opens inside your cheek, near your top back teeth. You can feel a tiny bump there with your tongue.

Here is the cool part. A nerve called the **facial nerve** runs right through the parotid gland, like a road through a forest. Inside the gland it splits into five branches, like fingers on a hand. Those branches make your face smile, blink and wrinkle your forehead. That's why surgeons are extra careful there.
levels.hs:
The **parotid gland** is the largest of the three pairs of major **salivary glands** (the others are the submandibular and sublingual glands). It sits in front of and below the ear, wrapped around the back edge of the jaw bone (the **ramus of the mandible**).

Its saliva is mostly watery (**serous**) and full of the enzyme amylase, which starts digesting starch. Saliva leaves through the **parotid duct** (Stensen's duct), which crosses the cheek muscle called the masseter, pierces the buccinator muscle, and opens opposite the **upper second molar tooth**.

The most important thing inside the parotid is the **facial nerve** (cranial nerve VII). It leaves the skull through the **stylomastoid foramen**, enters the gland, and splits into five branches that control the muscles of facial expression. A common memory trick, from top to bottom, is "**To Zanzibar By Motor Car**":
- Temporal
- Zygomatic
- Buccal
- Marginal mandibular
- Cervical

Importantly, the facial nerve does **not** make the parotid produce saliva. That job belongs to a different nerve, the glossopharyngeal (CN IX).

Real example: **mumps** is a viral infection that makes the parotid glands swell painfully, giving a chipmunk-cheek look. Because the gland is wrapped in a tight capsule, the swelling hurts.
levels.college:
**Location and relations.** The parotid occupies the retromandibular region: bounded by the zygomatic arch above, the external acoustic meatus and mastoid behind, and the masseter in front. It is enclosed by the **parotid fascia**, derived from the investing layer of deep cervical fascia, which explains why inflammation causes tense, painful swelling.

**Structures within the gland, superficial to deep:**
- **Facial nerve** (most superficial)
- **Retromandibular vein** (formed by the superficial temporal and maxillary veins)
- **External carotid artery**, which divides in the gland into the maxillary and superficial temporal arteries
- Parotid lymph nodes

**Facial nerve course.** After exiting the stylomastoid foramen, CN VII gives the posterior auricular nerve and branches to the posterior belly of digastric and stylohyoid. It then enters the gland and divides at the **pes anserinus** ("goose's foot") into temporofacial and cervicofacial trunks, then into the five terminal branches. The nerve plane is surgically used to divide the gland into **superficial and deep lobes**, although this is a surgical convention rather than a true anatomical lobe.

**Innervation of secretion.** The parasympathetic pathway is:
- Inferior salivatory nucleus → **glossopharyngeal nerve** → tympanic nerve (Jacobson's nerve) → tympanic plexus → **lesser petrosal nerve** → **otic ganglion** (synapse) → postganglionic fibres hitch a ride on the **auriculotemporal nerve** (a V3 branch) to the gland.
- Sympathetic fibres arrive from the superior cervical ganglion along the external carotid plexus.

**Duct.** Stensen's duct is about 5 cm long, runs roughly along the middle third of a line from the tragus to the midpoint of the upper lip, curves around the anterior border of masseter, pierces buccinator and opens at a papilla opposite the upper second molar.

**Clinical anchor.** A facial nerve lesion distal to the stylomastoid foramen (for example, from parotid tumour or surgery) paralyses facial muscles but spares taste and lacrimation, whose fibres leave the nerve earlier in the temporal bone.
levels.phd:
**Developmental and structural detail.** The parotid arises from oral ectoderm around the sixth week, but it encapsulates late, after the lymphatic system has formed. Lymph nodes therefore become trapped *within* the parenchyma. This explains why the parotid is unique among salivary glands in containing intraglandular nodes, and why it is a common site of metastasis from scalp and periauricular cutaneous cancers such as squamous cell carcinoma and melanoma. Secretory units are almost purely serous acini, which is why parotid saliva is watery and amylase-rich and why parotid stones are less common than submandibular stones.

**Branching variability.** Davis and colleagues' classic dissection series (1956) classified the extratemporal facial nerve into six branching patterns, types I–VI, depending on how the temporofacial and cervicofacial divisions interconnect. Anastomoses are frequent between the zygomatic and buccal branches. By contrast, the **marginal mandibular** and **temporal (frontal)** branches usually have few connections, so injury to them tends to cause lasting weakness. This is why surgeons regard these two as the most vulnerable branches.

**Branch courses relevant to function:**
- The temporal branch crosses the zygomatic arch within or just deep to the temporoparietal fascia (superficial temporal fascia). Pitanguy's line, running from about 0.5 cm below the tragus to about 1.5 cm above the lateral eyebrow, approximates its path.
- The marginal mandibular branch runs deep to platysma. It may dip below the inferior border of the mandible, especially posterior to the facial artery, which places it at risk in submandibular incisions.
- The cervical branch supplies platysma.

**Gustatory sweating.** After parotidectomy, cut postganglionic parasympathetic fibres from the auriculotemporal nerve can regenerate aberrantly into sympathetic cholinergic sweat glands of the overlying skin. The result is **Frey syndrome**: flushing and sweating of the cheek while eating. The Minor starch-iodine test reveals the affected area. With careful testing, subclinical Frey syndrome is detectable in a large proportion of patients after surgery, whereas symptomatic cases are much less frequent.

**Tumour epidemiology.** About 80% of salivary gland tumours arise in the parotid, and most of these are benign. The **pleomorphic adenoma** is the most common. **Warthin tumour** is strongly associated with smoking and is often bilateral. The rule of thumb that the smaller the gland, the higher the chance a tumour is malignant follows from this.
levels.expert:
**Surgical identification of the main trunk.** In parotidectomy, the trunk is found before any branch is risked. Classic landmarks include:
- The **tragal pointer**: the trunk lies roughly 1 cm deep and slightly anteroinferior to its tip.
- The tympanomastoid suture, from which the nerve emerges just deep and inferior.
- The posterior belly of digastric, whose upper border lies at about the level of the nerve.
- The styloid process, which lies deep to the nerve.

When anterograde dissection is impossible because of tumour or scarring, surgeons use **retrograde dissection** from a peripheral branch, such as the marginal mandibular branch near the facial vessels or the buccal branch along Stensen's duct. In revision surgery, mastoidectomy can expose the intratemporal segment instead.

**Extent of surgery.** For benign tumours, practice has shifted from routine superficial parotidectomy toward **extracapsular dissection** and partial superficial parotidectomy. These approaches aim to reduce facial weakness and Frey syndrome while keeping recurrence low. Pleomorphic adenoma has an incomplete pseudocapsule with pseudopods, so tumour spillage or enucleation predisposes to multinodular recurrence. Intraoperative continuous facial nerve monitoring is widely used, although it supplements rather than replaces anatomical identification.

**Postoperative nerve function.** Transient facial weakness is common after parotidectomy and is usually caused by neuropraxia from traction. Permanent paralysis is uncommon in primary benign surgery. House–Brackmann grading (I–VI) standardises reporting. For a sacrificed nerve, immediate cable grafting with the great auricular or sural nerve, or a masseteric-to-facial nerve transfer, gives the best reanimation outcomes. Treatment for Frey syndrome includes botulinum toxin injection into the affected skin, which blocks acetylcholine release at the sweat glands. Interposition layers such as SMAS flaps aim to prevent it.

**Diagnostic pitfalls.** Facial weakness with a parotid mass strongly suggests malignancy. Adenoid cystic carcinoma is particularly notorious for **perineural spread** along VII, sometimes reaching the temporal bone, so MRI review must follow the nerve proximally to the stylomastoid foramen and beyond. Fine-needle aspiration and ultrasound-guided core biopsy are standard workup. The Milan System now standardises how salivary cytology is reported.

**Open questions.** Two key questions remain open. One is the optimal extent of surgery for small benign tumours. The other is whether de-escalated surgery is safe for low-grade cancers. Molecular markers such as MAML2 fusion in mucoepidermoid carcinoma and PLAG1/HMGA2 rearrangements in pleomorphic adenoma are increasingly refining diagnosis and prognosis.

keyPoints: The parotid is the largest salivary gland and makes mostly serous, amylase-rich saliva
Stensen's duct pierces buccinator and opens opposite the upper second molar
CN VII exits the stylomastoid foramen and divides in the gland into five branches
Secretion is driven by CN IX via the lesser petrosal nerve, otic ganglion and auriculotemporal nerve
Within the gland, superficial to deep: facial nerve, retromandibular vein, external carotid artery
Frey syndrome and facial weakness are key complications of parotid surgery

lessons.title: Muscles of Mastication and the Infratemporal Fossa

levels.kid:
Put your fingers on the sides of your head, just above your ears, and bite down hard. Feel that bump? That is a chewing muscle called the **temporalis**. Now touch your cheek near the corner of your jaw and bite again. That bulge is the **masseter**, one of the strongest muscles for its size.

You have four chewing muscles on each side. Two are easy to feel. Two hide deep inside, behind your cheekbone, in a secret room called the **infratemporal fossa**.

That hidden room is like a busy hallway. Nerves and blood vessels travel through it to reach your teeth, tongue and face. All four chewing muscles get their orders from one nerve, a branch of the big face-feeling nerve.
levels.hs:
The **muscles of mastication** (chewing muscles) move the lower jaw, the **mandible**. There are four on each side:
- **Temporalis**: a fan-shaped muscle on the side of the skull. It closes the jaw, and its back fibers pull the jaw backward.
- **Masseter**: a thick muscle from the cheekbone (zygomatic arch) to the angle of the mandible. It is a powerful jaw closer.
- **Medial pterygoid**: a deep muscle that mirrors the masseter on the inner side of the jaw. It also closes the jaw.
- **Lateral pterygoid**: a deep muscle that pulls the jaw forward and helps open the mouth.

Notice that three muscles close the jaw and only one is a main opener. Biting needs force; opening mostly needs gravity and a little help.

All four are supplied by the **mandibular nerve (V3)**, the third branch of the **trigeminal nerve** (cranial nerve V). They develop from the **first pharyngeal arch**, which explains why one nerve controls them.

The two pterygoids sit in the **infratemporal fossa**, a space below the skull base and deep to the ramus of the mandible. It contains the **maxillary artery**, the **pterygoid venous plexus** and branches of V3.

A real example: a dentist numbing your lower teeth injects near the **inferior alveolar nerve**, which runs through this fossa before entering the mandible.
levels.college:
**Attachments and actions**
- **Temporalis**: from the temporal fossa and temporal fascia to the coronoid process and anterior ramus. Elevates; posterior, nearly horizontal fibers retract the mandible.
- **Masseter**: superficial and deep parts from the zygomatic arch to the lateral ramus and angle. Elevates; the superficial part helps protrude.
- **Medial pterygoid**: deep head from the medial surface of the lateral pterygoid plate, superficial head from the maxillary tuberosity, to the medial angle. With the masseter it forms a **pterygomasseteric sling** around the angle. Elevates, protrudes, and moves the jaw side to side.
- **Lateral pterygoid**: upper head from the infratemporal surface of the greater wing of the sphenoid, lower head from the lateral surface of the lateral pterygoid plate, to the **pterygoid fovea** of the condylar neck, the TMJ capsule and the disc. Protrudes and depresses; acting on one side, it swings the chin to the opposite side.

Depression is aided by gravity and the suprahyoid muscles (digastric, mylohyoid, geniohyoid).

**Innervation**: all by motor branches of **V3** (masseteric, deep temporal, nerves to the pterygoids). The nerve to the medial pterygoid also supplies tensor tympani and tensor veli palatini.

**Infratemporal fossa boundaries**
- Lateral: ramus of the mandible
- Medial: lateral pterygoid plate
- Anterior: posterior surface of the maxilla
- Roof: greater wing of the sphenoid, pierced by **foramen ovale** (V3) and **foramen spinosum** (middle meningeal artery)

**Contents**: lateral and medial pterygoids; the **maxillary artery** (1st and 2nd parts); the pterygoid venous plexus; V3 and its branches (inferior alveolar, lingual, buccal, auriculotemporal); the **chorda tympani** joining the lingual nerve; and the **otic ganglion** just below foramen ovale.
levels.phd:
**Developmental logic.** All four masticatory muscles derive from first-arch paraxial and cranial mesoderm, patterned by neural crest–derived connective tissue. Their innervation by the trigeminal motor root, which joins V3 in foramen ovale, reflects this origin. Tensor tympani and tensor veli palatini share it, while the arch-2 muscles (facial expression, stapedius, posterior digastric) take the facial nerve.

**Lateral pterygoid controversy.** The classic model held that the superior head is active in closing and stabilizes the disc, while the inferior head drives opening and protrusion. EMG studies and anatomical dissections (Juniper; Hannam and colleagues) have complicated this. The superior head inserts largely into the condylar neck, and only a variable fraction attaches to the disc. Fine-wire EMG suggests graded, task-dependent activity rather than strictly reciprocal heads. This matters for theories that blame disc displacement on lateral pterygoid hyperactivity, which remain unproven.

**Force architecture.** The masseter and medial pterygoid are multipennate with internal tendon sheets, so they pack many fibers into a small volume and produce high force over short excursions. Temporalis has longer fibers suited to positioning. Maximal human bite force at the molars is typically several hundred newtons. The sling and the jaw's geometry make the mandible behave as a lever, with the TMJ loaded during most bites.

**Fossa neurovascular relationships.**
- The maxillary artery runs superficial or deep to the lower head of the lateral pterygoid; the superficial course is more common in most populations. Its mandibular part gives the middle meningeal, accessory meningeal and inferior alveolar arteries. Its pterygoid part supplies the masticatory muscles and buccal artery.
- The auriculotemporal nerve splits around the middle meningeal artery. It carries postganglionic parasympathetic fibers from the otic ganglion (preganglionic from CN IX via the lesser petrosal nerve) toward the parotid.
- The chorda tympani exits the petrotympanic fissure to join the lingual nerve, adding taste fibers from the anterior two-thirds of the tongue and secretomotor fibers to the submandibular ganglion.
- The pterygoid venous plexus connects with the cavernous sinus through emissary veins of foramen ovale and the foramen of Vesalius, and with the facial vein via the deep facial vein.
levels.expert:
**Clinical consequences of a V3 lesion.** An isolated trigeminal motor lesion causes the jaw to deviate **toward the weak side** on opening, because the intact lateral pterygoid pushes the condyle forward unopposed. Temporalis and masseter wasting gives a hollowed temple and cheek. That contour change can be the first sign of a skull-base tumor along V3, such as a trigeminal schwannoma, nasopharyngeal carcinoma invading through foramen ovale, or perineural spread of a skin cancer. MRI showing **denervation changes** in the masticatory muscles is a valuable indirect marker of a V3 lesion.

**Surgical approaches.** The infratemporal fossa is a gateway to the lateral skull base. Fisch type C/D and preauricular subtemporal–infratemporal approaches displace or divide the zygoma and mandibular condyle, mobilize temporalis on its pedicle, and require controlling the maxillary artery and its venous plexus. Endoscopic endonasal routes, such as transpterygoid and transmaxillary extensions, now reach the same space from the medial side. Temporalis is also the workhorse for reconstruction: transposed flaps fill skull-base defects, and lengthening temporalis myoplasty restores a dynamic smile after facial palsy.

**Trismus.** Restricted opening has many causes: infection of the masticatory space, which often spreads from lower third molars; tumor infiltration of the pterygoids; radiation fibrosis after head and neck cancer therapy; and tetanus. New trismus in a patient with prior nasopharyngeal or oral cancer is presumed recurrence until imaging proves otherwise.

**Pitfalls.**
- Inferior alveolar nerve blocks can cause a transient facial palsy if the injection passes too deep into the parotid. They can also cause a hematoma if the needle enters the pterygoid plexus.
- Pterygoid plexus thrombophlebitis can propagate to the cavernous sinus.
- Mandibular ramus osteotomies (BSSO) risk the inferior alveolar and lingual nerves.

**Open questions.** Botulinum toxin injection into the masseter for bruxism and masseteric hypertrophy is common, but evidence for durable pain benefit is mixed, and it raises concerns about bone loss in the condyle. Whether lateral pterygoid dysfunction causes or follows disc derangement remains unresolved.

keyPoints: Four muscles of mastication: temporalis, masseter, medial and lateral pterygoid
Temporalis, masseter and medial pterygoid close the jaw
Lateral pterygoid protrudes the jaw and helps open it
All are first-arch muscles supplied by the mandibular nerve (V3)
The infratemporal fossa lies deep to the mandibular ramus, below the skull base
It contains the pterygoids, maxillary artery, pterygoid plexus and V3 branches

lessons.title: The Temporomandibular Joint: Structure and Movement

levels.kid:
Put your fingers just in front of your ears and open your mouth wide. Feel that bump moving? That is your **jaw joint**. Doctors call it the TMJ.

The TMJ is where your lower jaw meets your skull. You have two of them, one on each side, and they always work together like a team.

Inside each joint is a tiny soft pad, like a cushion. It sits between the bones so they don't rub.

The joint is special because it can do two moves. First it swings like a door hinge. Then, when you open really wide, the jaw slides forward too, like a drawer. That is how you can take a big bite of an apple!
levels.hs:
The **temporomandibular joint (TMJ)** connects the lower jaw (the **mandible**) to the **temporal bone** of the skull. You have one in front of each ear, and because the mandible is a single bone, the left and right joints always move together.

Key parts:
- The **condyle**: the rounded knob at the top of the mandible.
- The **mandibular fossa**: a shallow socket in the temporal bone, with a bump in front called the **articular eminence**.
- The **articular disc**: a pad of tough fibrocartilage between the bones. It splits the joint into an upper and a lower compartment.
- A **capsule** and ligaments, especially the **lateral (temporomandibular) ligament**, hold everything together.

The TMJ is a **synovial joint**. That means it has a fluid-filled space that lets the bones glide smoothly. Unusually, its surfaces are covered with fibrocartilage instead of the hyaline cartilage found in most joints.

Movement happens in two steps. In early opening the condyle **rotates** like a hinge. To open wide, the condyle and disc **slide forward** onto the articular eminence. This is called **translation**.

Real example: if someone yawns too widely, the condyle can slip in front of the eminence and get stuck. This is a **dislocated jaw**: the mouth is locked open until a clinician guides the condyle back down and backward.
levels.college:
The TMJ is a **bilateral, synovial, ginglymoarthrodial** joint: it combines hinge rotation (ginglymus) with gliding (arthrodia).

**Articular surfaces.** The mandibular condyle meets the mandibular fossa and articular eminence of the squamous temporal bone. The surfaces are lined with **dense fibrocartilage**, not hyaline cartilage. This reflects the joint's origin as a secondary cartilage joint and allows it to remodel.

**Disc and compartments.** The biconcave **articular disc** has a thin intermediate zone flanked by thicker anterior and posterior bands. It divides the joint into:
- **Superior compartment** (disc–temporal bone): handles translation.
- **Inferior compartment** (condyle–disc): handles rotation.
Behind the disc lies the **retrodiscal tissue** (bilaminar zone): an elastic superior lamina and a collagenous inferior lamina, with nerves and vessels between them. The disc is tied firmly to the condylar poles by collateral ligaments, so it travels with the condyle.

**Ligaments.**
- **Lateral (temporomandibular) ligament**: thickened lateral capsule. It is the main stabilizer and limits posterior displacement.
- **Sphenomandibular** (spine of sphenoid to lingula) and **stylomandibular** (styloid to angle) ligaments: accessory, with modest roles.

**Movements.**
- **Depression (opening)**: rotation in the lower compartment for roughly the first 20–25 mm of incisal opening, then translation forward. Driven by the lateral pterygoid with suprahyoid muscles and gravity.
- **Elevation**: masseter, temporalis and medial pterygoid.
- **Protrusion**: both lateral pterygoids. **Retrusion**: posterior temporalis fibres.
- **Lateral excursion**: one lateral pterygoid pulls its condyle forward (the orbiting side). The opposite condyle pivots in place (the working side).

**Innervation and blood supply.** Sensory supply comes mainly from the **auriculotemporal nerve**, with masseteric and deep temporal branches, all from V3. Blood comes from the superficial temporal and maxillary arteries.

Normal maximal opening is about 40–50 mm between the incisors.
levels.phd:
The TMJ's peculiarities trace to its development. Its condylar cartilage is a **secondary cartilage**, arising from periosteal progenitors independent of Meckel's cartilage. As a result, the condyle grows by appositional proliferation of a prechondroblastic layer, not by a classic growth plate. Unlike limb joints, the articular surface is covered by **fibrocartilage**, rich in type I collagen. Its superficial cells express **lubricin (PRG4)**, and in mice PRG4 loss causes TMJ osteoarthritis-like degeneration.

The disc is largely avascular and aneural in its intermediate zone. Its collagen fibres run anteroposteriorly in the centre and circumferentially in the bands. It is anisotropic and viscoelastic: under sustained clenching it creeps, and joint lubrication depends on boundary lubricants and phospholipids.

**Kinematics.** Classical teaching separates pure rotation from translation. However, jaw-tracking studies show that the condylar path is a continuous combination of both from early opening. The instantaneous centre of rotation therefore lies below the condyle, near the mandibular foramen. The often-cited rotation-only phase is an idealization. The articular eminence's slope (typically 30–60°) shapes the condylar path and steepens through childhood.

**Lateral pterygoid controversy.** The superior head inserts partly into the disc and capsule, and the inferior head into the condylar fovea. The proposal that the superior head acts reciprocally, active on closing to stabilize the disc against the eminence, came from EMG work by McNamara (1973). Later fine-wire studies (e.g., Murray and colleagues) suggest the heads function more as a graded continuum. The muscle's role in causing disc displacement remains unproven.

**Loading.** Finite-element and in vivo models indicate the TMJ is a load-bearing joint, not a frictionless link. Loading is greater on the side opposite the bite (the balancing side) during unilateral biting.

**Disc displacement.** In anterior disc displacement with reduction, the posterior band slips in front of the condyle. On opening the condyle passes beneath it, producing a reciprocal click. Without reduction, the disc blocks translation and opening is limited.
levels.expert:
**Temporomandibular disorders (TMD)** affect roughly 5–12% of adults and are more common in women. Classification now follows the **DC/TMD (2014)** criteria. Axis I covers physical diagnoses: myalgia, arthralgia, disc displacements and degenerative joint disease. Axis II assesses psychosocial status and pain-related disability. The prospective **OPPERA** cohort showed that first-onset TMD is predicted less by joint mechanics than by pain amplification, multiple comorbid pain conditions, and psychological factors. This reframes most TMD as a chronic overlapping pain condition rather than a purely structural problem.

Clinical pitfalls:
- **Imaging**: MRI (closed and open mouth, proton density) is the reference standard for disc position. However, disc displacement appears in about a third of asymptomatic people, so imaging findings must be matched to symptoms. CBCT is best for cortical erosion and condylar morphology.
- **Mimics**: preauricular pain can be referred from dental disease, otitis, or parotid pathology. In older adults, jaw claudication suggests **giant cell arteritis**, which is a vision-threatening emergency. Trismus with cranial neuropathies raises concern for infratemporal or skull-base malignancy.
- **Fractures**: condylar neck fractures are common after chin impact. The fragment is usually pulled anteromedially by the lateral pterygoid. Look for contralateral body or symphysis fractures. In children, closed management is favoured because the condyle remodels.

Surgical relevance: the TMJ lies in front of the external acoustic meatus and directly beneath the middle cranial fossa floor. The glenoid fossa roof can be thin, and condylar intrusion into the middle cranial fossa is a recognized complication after trauma. In preauricular approaches, the **temporal (frontal) branch of the facial nerve** crosses the zygomatic arch, and the auriculotemporal nerve and superficial temporal vessels lie in the field. Lateral skull-base approaches (infratemporal fossa type A) may displace or resect the condyle.

Treatment is stepwise. First-line care is conservative and includes education, physiotherapy, splints and behavioural therapy. Arthrocentesis is the next step for closed lock, and arthroscopy or open surgery is reserved for selected cases. For end-stage disease or **ankylosis**, total alloplastic joint replacement is an option. Gap arthroplasty with early aggressive mobilization helps prevent ankylosis from recurring.

Open questions: whether disc repositioning changes long-term outcomes, and how to bioengineer a disc replacement.

keyPoints: The TMJ links the mandibular condyle to the temporal bone's fossa and articular eminence
A fibrocartilage articular disc splits it into upper and lower compartments
Its articular surfaces are fibrocartilage, not hyaline cartilage
Opening combines hinge rotation (lower compartment) with forward translation (upper compartment)
The lateral pterygoid protrudes the jaw and drives opening; the lateral ligament is the main stabilizer
Sensory supply comes mainly from the auriculotemporal nerve (V3)

test.q: Which bone of the skull articulates with the mandible at the TMJ?
test.explain: The mandibular condyle sits in the mandibular fossa of the temporal bone. The sphenoid only gives attachment to an accessory ligament.

test.q: What covers the articular surfaces of the TMJ?
test.explain: Unlike most synovial joints, the TMJ is lined by dense fibrocartilage. Hyaline cartilage is the tempting wrong answer because it lines most joints.

test.q: Rotation of the condyle during early opening mainly occurs in which compartment?
test.explain: The condyle turns against the disc in the lower compartment. The disc–temporal (upper) compartment handles translation.

test.q: Which muscle protrudes the mandible when both sides contract?
test.explain: Both lateral pterygoids pull the condyles forward. The other three are mainly elevators.

test.q: Which ligament is the main stabilizer of the TMJ?
test.explain: The lateral (temporomandibular) ligament is the thickened lateral capsule. The other two named ligaments are only accessory.

test.q: During a wide yawn, the condyle slips anterior to the articular eminence and the mouth stays open. This is:
test.explain: Anterior dislocation traps the condyle in front of the eminence, locking the mouth open.

test.q: Which nerve gives most sensory supply to the TMJ?
test.explain: The auriculotemporal branch of V3 is the main sensory nerve, helped by masseteric and deep temporal branches.

test.q: Which muscles mainly elevate (close) the jaw?
test.explain: The three classic elevators close the mouth. The suprahyoids and lateral pterygoids help open it.

test.q: In lateral excursion to the right, which condyle moves forward?
test.explain: The left lateral pterygoid pulls the left (orbiting) condyle forward, while the right (working) condyle pivots in place.

test.q: The forward sliding of the condyle and disc onto the eminence is called ___.
test.explain: Translation occurs in the superior compartment and allows wide opening.

test.q: What is the bump of temporal bone in front of the mandibular fossa called?
test.explain: The condyle glides onto the articular eminence when the mouth opens wide.

test.q: The TMJ combines hinge and gliding motion, so it is described as ___.
test.explain: Ginglymus means hinge and arthrodia means gliding.

kidTest.q: Where can you feel your jaw joint?
choices: At the back of your neck
Just in front of your ears
kidTest.explain: The TMJ sits right in front of each ear.

kidTest.q: What is inside the joint between the bones?
kidTest.explain: A pad called the disc keeps the bones from rubbing.

kidTest.q: How many jaw joints do you have?
kidTest.explain: You have one on each side, and they work as a team.

kidTest.q: When you open really wide, the jaw also:
kidTest.explain: It slides forward like a drawer after first swinging like a hinge.

kidTest.q: The first jaw move swings like a door h _ _ _ _.
kidTest.explain: Opening starts with a hinge-like swing.

advancedTest.q: Why is the condylar cartilage able to remodel after a childhood condylar fracture?
choices: It derives directly from Meckel's cartilage, which persists for life
It lacks a synovial lining, so there is no inflammatory scarring
It is a secondary fibrocartilage growing appositionally from progenitors
It is a primary hyaline growth plate that has not yet fused
advancedTest.explain: The condyle grows by appositional proliferation of secondary cartilage, which allows remodeling. This is why closed management is favoured in children.

advancedTest.q: A patient has a reciprocal click on opening and closing with normal range. The most likely disc state is:
choices: Normal disc resting on the eminence
advancedTest.explain: With reduction, the condyle passes under the displaced posterior band and clicks. Without reduction, opening is limited.

advancedTest.q: Why should MRI disc displacement not alone drive surgery?
choices: CBCT is the reference standard for disc position
Displacement is common in people without symptoms
Disc position changes too fast for MRI to capture
MRI is not able to show the disc in most patients
advancedTest.explain: About a third of asymptomatic people show displacement, so imaging findings must be matched to the clinical picture.

advancedTest.q: What did the OPPERA cohort imply about first-onset TMD?
choices: Its onset is predicted mainly by eminence slope and disc position
Its onset is predicted strongly by pain amplification and psychosocial factors
It arises mainly from lateral pterygoid hyperactivity seen on EMG
It follows mainly from condylar fractures sustained in childhood
advancedTest.explain: OPPERA found central pain sensitivity, comorbid pain conditions and psychological factors to be key predictors. This supports a chronic overlapping pain model.
